What you get Plugin-only Template / Sync Full repo checkout Skills (16 workflow and utility skills) Y Y Y Profiles (language-specific) Y Y Y Commands Y (Claude) Y (Claude) Y Hooks Y (Claude) Y Y Sub-agents Y (Claude) Y Y Config (settings/rules) Y Y Statusline Y Y Template sync infrastructure Y Y Generation tools / tests Y

Plugin-only (Claude): /plugin install kk@claude-toolbox — skills, commands, hooks, agents, profiles.

Plugin-only (Codex): codex plugin marketplace add serpro69/claude-toolbox — skills and profiles only. Hooks, agents, rules, and config require template setup.

Template / Sync: Full configuration for both providers, kept in sync with upstream via GitHub Actions.

Full repo checkout: Everything above plus the generation tools (cmd/), test suites (test/), and maintainer workflows.

docs.title: Marketplace gotchas
docs.text:
Plugin source paths must use "./", not "." In marketplace.json, the source field for each plugin entry must use "./" (with trailing slash) for repo-root plugins, not bare ".". Claude Code's path resolver does not treat them equivalently — "." causes plugin install to fail with a misleading "source type not supported" error. Paths to subdirectories (e.g., "./klaude-plugin") already include the "./" prefix and are unaffected.

Stale marketplace cache after fixing. Claude Code caches cloned marketplace repos under ~/.claude/plugins/. After fixing marketplace.json and pushing, marketplace add or marketplace update may still use the stale cache. For a clean slate: remove the marketplace entry from ~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/<name>/, delete any references in ~/.claude/plugins/known_marketplaces.json and ~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json, then re-add with claude plugin marketplace add.

docs.title: Skill execution
docs.text:
User invokes /kk:review-code
  → Claude Code loads SKILL.md (${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} substituted)
  → Skill reads shared instructions via symlinks
  → Profile detection runs (git diff --stat → DETECTION.md matching)
  → Profile content loaded (index.md → always-load + conditional files)
  → Subject-matter action (read diff, produce findings)

docs.title: Template sync
docs.text:
Downstream repo triggers sync workflow
  → Sparse-clones upstream at specified version
  → Reads .github/template-state.json for variables and exclusions
  → Copies .claude/, .codex/ to staging
  → Applies variable substitutions (CC_MODEL, CODEX_MODEL, etc.)
  → Smart-merges settings.json except permissions.deny (replaced from upstream)
  → Reports removed deny entries; leaves project kk-guard.json alone
  → Creates PR with changes

docs.title: Documentation publishing
docs.text:
Push to master
  → .github/workflows/docs.yml triggers
  → mike deploy --push dev (unreleased docs)

Push tag v0.14.0
  → .github/workflows/docs.yml triggers
  → Extracts major.minor → "0.14"
  → mike deploy --push --update-aliases "0.14" latest
  → mike set-default --push latest (bare URL → latest release)
  → GitHub Pages serves from gh-pages branch

docs.title: Codex generation
docs.text:
make generate-kodex
  → go test (unit tests for generation tool)
  → go run cmd/generate-kodex -manifest scripts/kodex-generate-manifest.yml
    → Copy skills with ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} → relative path transform
    → Copy profiles as-is
    → Convert agents/*.md → agents/*.toml
    → Generate .codex-plugin/plugin.json
  → make test-structure (validate bidirectional invariants)

docs.title: ADRs
docs.text:
Architecture decisions are recorded in docs/adr/:

ADR Decision 0001 Profile detection model (path → filename → content signals) 0002 Profile content organization (per-phase subdirectories) 0003 Plugin-root referenced content (no symlinks into profiles) 0004 Skill workflow ordering (instructions before action) 0005 Codex hook enforcement gap (advisory + hook two-layer approach) 0012 Single permission declaration, generated projections and scoped guard configuration

docs.title: Plugin Development
docs.text: The kk plugin lives at klaude-plugin/. This section covers the practical rules for authoring each component. For the full specification, see CLAUDE.md.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text: Each skill is a directory under klaude-plugin/skills/<name>/ containing at minimum a SKILL.md entry point.

docs.title: SKILL.md structure
docs.text:
---
name: skill-name
description: |
  Trigger-first description. Front-load the key use case.
---

# Skill Title

## Conventions
## Workflow

docs.title: Naming rules
docs.text:
• Imperative verbs over noun phrases: /kk:design not /kk:analysis-process.
  • Family prefixes for grouped skills: /kk:review-code, /kk:review-design, /kk:review-spec.
  • Always use /kk: prefix when referencing skills: write /kk:review-code not review-code. The codex generation tool rewrites /kk: → $kk: for Codex output.

docs.title: Description budget
docs.text: Claude Code truncates skill descriptions at 1,536 characters per entry. OpenCode's limit is 1,024. Lead with trigger keywords — truncation happens at the tail. Detailed rules, cascades, and examples belong in the SKILL.md body, not the description.

docs.title: Workflow ordering (ADR 0004)
docs.text:
Every skill MUST fully load its instructions before taking any action on its subject matter. This is the single most critical rule for skill authoring.

  • "Instructions" = SKILL.md + referenced process files + shared protocols + resolved profile content.
  • "Action on subject matter" = reading diff content, editing code, engaging with idea prose, running tests, producing findings.
  • A narrow early scope is permitted (e.g., git diff --stat for filenames) to drive profile detection.
  • Content-level read instructions appear exactly once in the workflow, after instruction loading.

Every skill's Workflow section must carry a mandatory-order directive at the top naming this rule by intent. The failure mode: once an LLM has diff content loaded, it has enough to pattern-match findings without methodology, and its efficiency bias favors the shortcut. The methodology becomes ceremony the agent optimizes away.

docs.title: Shared Instructions
docs.text:
Instructions consumed by multiple skills live at klaude-plugin/skills/_shared/<name>.md. Each consuming skill gets a symlink:

# In the consuming skill directory:
ln -s ../_shared/<name>.md shared-<name>.md

Reference in skill prose as [shared-<name>.md](shared-<name>.md). The shared- prefix makes it obvious which files are shared vs. skill-specific. Only symlink into skills that actually reference the file.

Symlinks must stay inside the skills/ tree — cross-boundary symlinks break under some plugin installers (see ADR 0003).

docs.title: Plugin Content Is Self-Contained
docs.text: klaude-plugin/ ships standalone via the plugin marketplace — consumers get the plugin tree only, never this repo's docs/. Skill, agent, and profile prose must never reference toolbox-repo documents: no "(ADR NNNN)" citations, no links into this repo's docs/adr/ or docs/feat/wip|done/. For a consumer these are unresolvable at best; at worst they collide with the consumer repo's own ADR numbering and point to unrelated decisions. State each rule and its rationale in full in the plugin file itself; the back-reference lives on the repo side (the ADR cites the operative plugin files, not the other way around). Consumer-repo paths as behavioral targets (e.g. /kk:review-architecture accepting artifacts from the consumer's docs/adr/) are correct and expected.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Commands live under klaude-plugin/commands/<name>/. For skills with standard + isolated modes:

  • default.md — standard variant, invoked as /kk:<name>:default
  • isolated.md — isolated sub-agent variant, invoked as /kk:<name>:isolated

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
Agent definitions live at klaude-plugin/agents/<name>.md with frontmatter specifying name, description, and tools (an allowlist of tools the agent can use):

---
name: code-reviewer
description: |
  Independent code reviewer with no authorship attachment.
tools:
  - Read
  - Grep
  - Glob
  - mcp__capy__capy_search
---

Agent names describe the role (code-reviewer, design-reviewer), not the skill that invokes them. Don't rename agent files when renaming skills.

Agents inherit the instruction-before-action rule — they must read provided checklists before analyzing subject matter, regardless of payload delivery order from the spawning skill.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
Hook definitions in klaude-plugin/hooks/hooks.json:

{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "bash ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/set-plugin-root.sh ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}"
      }]
    }],
    "PreToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Bash|Read|Edit|Write|NotebookEdit|Grep|Glob|mcp__.+__capy_(execute|execute_file|batch_execute)",
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/guard/guard.sh",
        "timeout": 15,
        "onFailure": "block"
      }]
    }]
  }
}

SessionStart hook: Exports TOOLBOX_PLUGIN_ROOT into the session via $CLAUDE_ENV_FILE. A standalone resolver (cpr.py) reads installed_plugins.json to find the install that applies to the current project (passed as $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR); the harness-substituted ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, passed as an argument, is the fallback. Once set, every Bash tool call in the session has ${TOOLBOX_PLUGIN_ROOT} available — this gives LLMs a reliable path to the plugin root without guessing.

Permission guard contract: Read the complete hook payload from stdin (tool_name, tool_input, cwd and optional permission_mode). scripts/guard/guard.sh buffers the bytes once and invokes guard.py under isolated Python. Ordinary allow is silent with exit 0; config warnings may emit only systemMessage. Deny emits hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision: "deny", its reason on stdout and stderr, and exit 2. Missing interpreters, crashes and invalid engine output must deny. Claude's onFailure: "block" handles hook launch failures and timeouts; it requires Claude Code 2.1.295+. See the configuration guide for runtime requirements and supported channels.

The declaration and engine in klaude-plugin/scripts/guard/ are canonical. Run make generate-guard after changing them; never edit .codex/scripts/guard/, .codex/rules/default.rules, or the marked rules tables directly. The generator also owns .claude/settings.json's permissions.deny, leaving other settings unchanged. Keep the copied license with the engine.

To develop this repository with an agent, the user adds a physical checkout path (or a parent covering worktrees) to ~/.claude/kk-guard.json:

{"version":1,"projects":{"/absolute/path/to/claude-toolbox":{"disable_selfmod":true}}}

Merge that entry into existing user configuration. This permits settings and guard-file edits without disabling secrets checks. The project file can only tighten policy; committing disable_selfmod there does not authorize edits. Without the user exception, even adding a permission allow entry to settings is blocked. Destructive operations remain governed by their separate category settings and Codex native rules.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
Profiles at klaude-plugin/profiles/<name>/ provide domain-specific content to every workflow phase. See the Profile Conventions section of CLAUDE.md for the full specification.

Required files:

  • DETECTION.md — three mandatory section headings: ## Path signals, ## Filename signals, ## Content signals. All three must be present even if the body is empty. Optional: ## Design signals for pre-code detection.
  • overview.md — human-readable summary and dependency-lookup targets.

Phase subdirectories: review-code/, design/, implement/, test/, document/, review-spec/. Not every profile populates every phase. Each populated phase must have an index.md with always-load and conditional entries. Conditional entries need explicit Load if: clauses naming concrete diff properties — two agents evaluating the same diff must reach the same conclusion.

Bidirectional index invariant (enforced by test/test-plugin-structure.sh):

  • Forward: every markdown link in index.md resolves to a file on disk.
  • Reverse: every .md in the phase directory (except index.md) is referenced by the index.

An unreferenced .md inside a phase subdirectory is always a bug. Authoring notes belong in overview.md at the profile root, not inside phase subdirectories.

Adding a new profile checklist:

  1. Create the profile directory by copying an existing one as a template.
  2. Write DETECTION.md and overview.md.
  3. Populate the phase subdirectories the profile needs (each with index.md).
  4. Append the profile name to EXPECTED_PROFILES in test/test-plugin-structure.sh.
  5. Append the profile name to the Known Profiles list in klaude-plugin/skills/_shared/profile-detection.md.
  6. Run bash test/test-plugin-structure.sh and confirm green.

docs.title: Evaluations
docs.text:
Skills with non-trivial decision logic should ship evaluation scenarios under klaude-plugin/skills/<skill>/evals/. One directory per eval:

evals/<eval-name>/
  eval.json        # scenario definition
  test-files/      # real filesystem fixtures

eval.json schema:

{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "eval-name-kebab-case",
  "description": "What this eval tests.",
  "skills": ["skill-name"],
  "prompt": "The user prompt that triggers the skill.",
  "trap": "The failure hypothesis — what a model is likely to get wrong.",
  "files": ["test-files/foo.yaml"],
  "assertions": [
    { "id": "1.1", "text": "Specific, gradable behavior." }
  ]
}

Use real filesystem fixtures in test-files/, not inline JSON strings. Include at least one regression eval proving the skill does NOT activate when it shouldn't.

docs.title: ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} — Substitution Rules
docs.text:
The harness provides ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} resolving to the installed plugin's root. Understanding its substitution boundary is critical (ADR 0003):

Substituted at plugin-load time (safe to use freely):

  • SKILL.md files
  • agents/*.md files
  • hooks/*.json command strings
  • MCP config files

NOT substituted by the Read tool (the literal token reaches the agent):

  • Everything in skills/_shared/
  • Everything in profiles/
  • Any file an agent reads at runtime

For runtime-read files, prefer explicit content (e.g., hard-coded profile name lists) over the token. If the file must describe a plugin-root path, instruct the agent to construct it using the resolved prefix it already knows from SKILL.md.

TOOLBOX_PLUGIN_ROOT — runtime alternative. The SessionStart hook exports this env var into every Bash call. Unlike ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} (which is only substituted at plugin-load time), ${TOOLBOX_PLUGIN_ROOT} is available in the shell environment throughout the session. Use it in Bash commands when you need the plugin root at runtime — e.g., ls ${TOOLBOX_PLUGIN_ROOT}/profiles/.

Other rules:

  • Brace form required: ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} works, bare $CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT does NOT get substituted.
  • Glob won't work against these paths — it's cwd-scoped and returns 0 matches for outside-cwd absolute paths. Use Read with the resolved path instead.
  • To reference the variable name literally in prose, use bare $CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT or ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}.

docs.title: Capy Knowledge Protocol
docs.text:
Skills that interact with capy MCP tools use kk: namespaced source labels:

Label Contents kk:arch-decisions Architecture decisions, design rationale kk:review-findings Code review patterns, recurring issues kk:lang-idioms Language best practices from external sources kk:project-conventions Discovered project patterns kk:test-patterns Testing approaches, edge cases kk:debug-context Root causes, tricky bugs

Only index non-obvious learnings not derivable from reading the code or git history. Empty results are normal for new projects — proceed with standard guidelines.

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Workflow ordering is the #1 failure mode. If the agent sees subject matter before methodology, it shortcuts the methodology. Structure every workflow so instructions load first. See ADR 0004.

  2. Forgetting make generate-kodex. After editing anything in klaude-plugin/, the Codex variant drifts. CI checks this with make generate-kodex && git diff --exit-code kodex-plugin/ .codex/agents/.

  3. Orphan files in profile phase directories. Every .md file (except index.md) must be referenced by the phase's index.md. The bidirectional invariant test catches this.

  4. Symlinks outside skills/. Per-skill symlinks must point within the skills/ tree (../_shared/<name>.md). Cross-boundary symlinks break under some installers. Profile content uses ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} references instead.

  5. Skill description truncation. Descriptions are truncated from the tail. If your trigger keywords are at the end, the skill won't be matched. Lead with the use case.

  6. Stale Known Profiles list. When adding a profile, you must update both EXPECTED_PROFILES in the test file and the Known Profiles list in klaude-plugin/skills/_shared/profile-detection.md. The list is the runtime enumeration — consumers iterate it rather than walking the filesystem.

  7. Renaming skills. Update EXPECTED_SKILLS / EXPECTED_COMMANDS in tests. Don't rename agent files. Don't touch run_plugin_migration's dirs_to_remove in .claude/toolbox/scripts/template-sync.sh (historical cleanup paths). Don't touch docs/feat/done/ (frozen history). Watch for substring collisions in sed operations.

  8. Vague Load if: clauses. Conditional entries in profile index.md must name concrete diff properties (field values, filenames, directory names) — not vague category labels. Two agents evaluating the same diff must reach the same conclusion.

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text:
Run all test suites:

Use the project tools on your normal PATH. The structure checks need Python 3.11+ (tomllib) or the documented tomli fallback; template suites need Mike Farah's yq as well as jq. When selecting another Python installation, prepend its directory instead of replacing PATH and hiding existing tools.

for test in test/test-*.sh; do $test; done

Run a single suite:

./test/test-plugin-structure.sh

docs.title: Test Suites
docs.text: Suite What it covers test-plugin-structure.sh Plugin/marketplace manifests, skills, commands, hooks, profiles, cross-references, kodex-plugin generated output validation test-codex-structure.sh Codex marketplace, config.toml, hooks.json, agent TOMLs, Starlark rules, scripts, AGENTS.md test-template-sync.sh CLI parsing, manifest validation, variable substitution, settings merge, plugin migration, sync exclusions, self-update handoff test-template-cleanup.sh Manifest generation, variable capture, git tag/SHA detection test-claude-extra.sh CLAUDE.extra.md headings, CLAUDE.md imports of behavioral and AGENTS.md project instructions, compare_files detection, auto-import test-manifest-jq.sh JSON generation patterns, special character handling, schema validation, round-trip test-semver-compare.sh Semver comparison logic used by release workflows test-cpr.sh Claude Plugin Root resolver — exact/fuzzy matching, project-path resolution cascade (project → user → last-installed), install-path validation, env var precedence, error handling test-guard.sh Python engine tests: glob/path semantics, shell parsing, configuration layers, patches, capy inputs and corpus replay test-hooks.sh Full guard wrapper transport, plugin-only protection, fail-closed cases, capy-wrapper degradation, Read/Bash p95 latency test-generate-guard.sh Generated settings/rules/docs, output stability, per-rule examples and invalid-marker rejection test-codex-hooks.sh Bash/patch/MCP adapter delegation, failure denial, protected-files advisory and per-event capy handoff test-review-eval-staging.sh Fresh before/after/history and legacy fixture staging, path safety and evaluator-material exclusion test-review-instructions.sh Instruction-packet source completeness, routing inputs and path boundaries; does not establish actor compliance test-functional-review-tools.sh Extracted bundle/capture/receipt/grading utilities and archive inventory; runs from a temporary copy without historical evidence, using Python 3.11+

docs.title: Test Infrastructure
docs.text:
Tests use shared utilities from test/helpers.sh:

  • log_section, log_test — structured output
  • assert_equals, assert_contains, assert_file_exists — assertion helpers
  • log_pass, log_fail, log_skip — result reporting
  • print_summary — final pass/fail count

Test fixtures live in test/fixtures/. The retained functional-review utilities own small synthetic fixtures within their tests. Set FUNCTIONAL_REVIEW_PYTHON to an explicit Python 3.11+ interpreter when the default python3 is older. Codex hook cases derive from toolbox-only-hooks.json, so the legacy case stays independent of Capy registrations in the developer's live .codex/hooks.json.

docs.title: Writing Tests
docs.text:
Follow proportionate verification when choosing coverage and acceptance criteria; ADR 0010 records the rationale. Deterministic tests protect software contracts. Agent evaluations measure semantic outcomes with variability and evidence limits; each assertion is not automatically a release gate. Keep required repository checks, and expand verification only for a concrete risk or unresolved decision.

  • Add tests to the appropriate existing suite when possible
  • New suites follow the same pattern: source helpers.sh, use log_section/log_test/assert_*, end with print_summary
  • Structure tests check file existence and content invariants, not runtime behavior
  • The bidirectional index invariant (every link in index.md resolves, every .md in a phase dir is referenced) is enforced in test-plugin-structure.sh — adding profile content automatically gets tested

docs.title: Go Tests
docs.text:
The Go tools under cmd/ ship unit and integration tests:

go test ./cmd/generate-kodex/...   # Codex generation tool
go test ./cmd/plugin-graph/...     # plugin dependency-graph analyzer

cmd/generate-kodex tests also run as part of make generate-kodex.

cmd/plugin-graph tests run via make plugin-graph, which additionally runs go run ./cmd/plugin-graph --root klaude-plugin/ validate against the real plugin — a structural-health gate that exits non-zero on broken markdown/template links or orphaned content. It complements test-plugin-structure.sh's bidirectional index invariant: the structure test enforces profile index.md completeness, while plugin-graph validate catches broken links and orphans across the whole plugin. See Architecture › Plugin Graph Analysis.

docs.title: Validation Before Release
docs.text:
• Every test/test-*.sh suite must pass
  • make generate-kodex must leave kodex-plugin/ and .codex/agents/ clean (git diff --exit-code)
  • make generate-guard must leave .claude/settings.json, .codex/rules/, .codex/scripts/guard/ and docs/user-guide/configuration.md clean (git diff --exit-code)
  • make plugin-graph must pass (Go tests + validate exits 0 against klaude-plugin/)
  • Go tests must pass (go test ./...)

docs.title: Permission Guard Verification
docs.text:
Run the engine and wrapper separately when diagnosing a failure:

bash test/test-guard.sh
bash test/test-hooks.sh
bash test/test-codex-hooks.sh
bash test/test-generate-guard.sh

test/guard/test_guard.py imports the engine and replays test/fixtures/guard/corpus.jsonl. Rows carry expected decisions/categories, optional cwd/project roots and per-row configuration fixtures. They use a synthetic home and project; submitted commands are never executed. KK_GUARD_TEST_PYTHON selects the engine test interpreter. The Python floor is 3.8, with actual local runs on 3.9.6/macOS and 3.10.12/Linux; the 3.8 syntax check does not replace a 3.8 runtime run.

The wrapper suite times 100 Read calls and every active Bash corpus row, including process startup, validation and cleanup. It always reports both p95 values when the timing probes run. Targets are 30 ms for file tools and 50 ms for Bash; local gates fail at 60/100 ms respectively when CI is unset. With CI present, timing is reported without enforcement. A CI-mode pass is not evidence that a local latency target passed.

The 2026-10-26 macOS arm64 run with the default Apple Python 3.9.6 measured 76.62 ms Read / 76.00 ms Bash outside the agent sandbox: the Read gate failed and both targets were missed. The performance requirement remains open before feature completion; limits were not relaxed. See the permission-guard evidence for all attempts and prerequisites.

A later wrapper optimization on the same host prefers an existing Homebrew Python, skips unused site startup and avoids subprocesses for empty output. That run measured 40.92 ms Read / 42.13 ms Bash, passing both unchanged local gates and the Bash target. A second pass imports the engine through a small launcher so Python can reuse compiled bytecode: the unchanged benchmark measured 37.27 → 31.10 ms Read / 42.50 → 34.75 ms Bash against its immediate predecessor. The 30 ms Read target remains open. Earlier measurements remain historical evidence.

Launcher tests cover policy reloads between calls, unavailable caches, import isolation, source updates and loader failures. Cold starts and unwritable cache directories compile source. Apple Python 3.9.6 disables cache writes by default; its functional tests pass, with the corrupt-cache test explicitly skipped. The speedup was measured with Homebrew Python 3.15.1 and does not establish timing on other runtimes or hosts.

Final verification on Linux after the shell-path and escaped-literal corrections passed 96 engine tests on Python 3.10 and 3.12, the complete wrapper suite (51 cases / 248 assertions), and Codex adapter checks. Read/Bash p95 measured 23.66/41.59 ms with the unchanged local gates. The new regressions fail against the preceding engine and cover relative directory changes, wildcard matches and escaped interpreter paths, alongside benign and quoted/raw-literal controls. The current corrected engine still needs macOS timing; the user explicitly retained the 30 ms requirement.

Payload tests establish adapter contracts, not installed hook activation. Live probes must record versions, actual hook inputs/results and benign controls. The Claude bypass probe uses a disposable project outside temporary roots so rm -rf ./scratch is not intentionally exempt. Use synthetic files and an absent .env, never real credentials. The recorded Claude 2.1.296 probe denied both destructive and secrets access under bypass mode.

Codex 0.164.0 on macOS verified relative patch paths against cwd, first with inline hooks and then with project-file registration under normal config loading. The latter probe recorded one startup and two patch-hook invocations: the benign patch succeeded and the synthetic .env patch was denied. It used explicit project trust and a one-invocation hook-trust bypass for inspected definitions; persisted trust, interactive hook approval, restarts and other versions or hosts were not exercised. Two fresh --ignore-user-config probes recorded no hooks, including one with hooks explicitly enabled, so use normal config loading for this check. The isolated-mode cause remains tracked in #179 and the interactive trust lifecycle in #182; the full evidence and historical failed attempts remain in the feature's design §16.

docs.title: Agent evaluation
docs.text:
Skill evals live under each canonical klaude-plugin/skills/<skill>/evals/ directory. A scenario contains eval.json, subject files under test-files/ and optional grader-only expected results under oracle/. Regenerate the Codex copies with make generate-kodex.

The review harness describes component grading and full-workflow capture. Its setup.sh stages flat fixtures, complete before/ and after/ snapshots, and optional local Git history into fresh destinations. Use a workspace outside any SKILL.md ancestor so the host skill does not activate a profile on unrelated fixtures. Stage only subject files; keep assertions, oracles, grading controls and results outside actor inputs and filtered plugin bundles. Deliberately broken eval/template links must remain.

Run ordinary skill prompts against declared immutable instructions and fresh fixture/knowledge state. For targeted changes, compare with the immediate predecessor under matching conditions. Capture observable tool results, reviewer handoffs, initial/final files and final reports; do not substitute private reasoning or final self-attestation for execution. Never include credentials. Workflow grading uses sealed evidence; component grading uses the supplied output text. Calibrate the chosen grader against meaningful positive, negative and missing-evidence examples before making comparative claims.

Keep PASS/FAIL/PARTIAL observations separate from adoption. A material wrong verdict matters differently from optional advice, a missing endpoint name or an unavailable external reviewer. Retain all attempts and disclose sample size, runtime/configuration differences and missing coverage. Synthetic external-review replays test reporting, not live integration. Expand measurement only for a concrete uncertainty that could change the decision; structural tests do not establish model reliability.

The functional-review summary records the retained comparisons, current acceptance and known limits. Detailed captures remain in the feature's evidence tree until the human-owned release archive is verified.

1. Install the kk plugin to get all skills, commands, and hooks:

  2. Set up sync infrastructure. Create .github/template-state.json:

    {
  "schema_version": "1",

  "template_version": "v1.0.0",
  "synced_at": "1970-01-01T00:00:00Z",

  3. Run Template Sync from your repo's Actions tab to pull in the configuration (settings, statusline, permissions). Review and merge the PR.

Tip

Step 1 works standalone if you only want the skills. Steps 2-3 add the opinionated configuration and keep it in sync with upstream improvements.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
claude-toolbox is a collection of "tools" for all your agentic workflows (currently supports claude-code and codex!) — pre-configured MCP servers, skills, sub-agents, commands, hooks, statuslines with themes, and more — everything you need for AI-powered development workflows, used and battle-tested daily on many of my own projects.

Important

This project was created with the help of Claude-Code. It is, however, always reviewed, tested, and reworked with a human-in-the-loop.

No AI slop here. Purely AI-made skills are hot garbage, and that's putting it mildly.

That said, if you have any problems with code that is written by AI — you've been warned. But, then again, why would you be interested in AI-related configs and skills in the first place... ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

docs.title: Why claude-toolbox?
docs.text:
Tools like Claude Code and Codex are powerful on their own, but LLMs don't know your development workflow. This project started as a way to streamline configurations across projects without copy-paste. Over time, recurring patterns evolved into skills and agents.

A minimal, opinionated configuration — sensible permission baselines, a rich statusline, MCP server wiring, and sync infrastructure to keep it all up to date across your projects. Think of it as a dotfiles repo for Claude Code and Codex.

A structured development pipeline — 16 workflow and utility skills with explicit multi-language support that take you from idea through design, implementation, code review, testing, to documentation, with persistent knowledge that carries across sessions.

/kk:design → /kk:review-design → /kk:implement → /kk:review-code → /kk:test → /kk:document

docs.title: Features at a Glance
docs.text:
• 16 workflow and utility skills — a complete development pipeline invoked as /kk:<skill-name>, plus utilities such as /kk:clarify-docs for existing documentation, PR drafts and issue descriptions
  • Multi-language support — precise and distinct instructions from design, to implementation, to testing, to review for: Go, Java, JS/TS, Kotlin, Kubernetes, and Python
  • Multi-model code review — independent reviewers using sub-agents and external models (Gemini, etc.)
  • Persistent knowledge base — findings, decisions, and conventions that survive across sessions via Capy
  • Up-to-date library docs — always-current documentation lookup via Context7
  • Battle-tested configuration — permissions, statusline themes, hooks, sensible defaults

docs.title: kk Plugin
docs.text:
The kk plugin contains all development workflow functionality — 16 skills, 5 commands, and hooks — distributed via the Claude Code plugin system (see kodex-plugin for the Codex variant). Skills are invoked as /kk:skill-name, commands as /kk:dir:command.

Alongside skills/, commands/, agents/, and hooks/, the plugin ships a top-level profiles/ directory. Each profile (e.g., go, python, k8s) bundles per-domain content — detection rules, review checklists, design prompts, test validators, doc rubrics — that the workflow skills consult when the code under work matches the profile. Profiles are the extension point for new languages and IaC DSLs.

For an existing bug report or feature request, optionally use /kk:clarify-docs with a local draft, pasted description or issue URL. docs.title: Permission Guard
docs.text:
For an existing installation, follow the permission-guard upgrade checklist. Template consumers update both the installed plugin and project configuration; plugin-only consumers update the plugin. Restart to load the new runtime.

The plugin enforces its shipped baseline without template settings or guard config files. It covers Bash, Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit, and capy's three execution tools. Template installations additionally receive generated Read(...) secrets deny rules as a native fallback. Logs, build output, dependencies and .env.example are readable under the baseline.

Use Claude Code 2.1.295+ with Bash, jq and Python 3.8+. The wrapper denies when it cannot evaluate a call, and the hook registration blocks failures/timeouts. Destructive rules apply in bypass mode too. Turning hooks off removes destructive and self-modification protection; plugin-only installations also lose the hook's secrets protection.

Project config can tighten protection; only the user's config can loosen destructive rules or permit settings edits. See Guard Configuration for examples, including the disable_selfmod entry needed when an agent edits settings. Secrets remain protected; search-result contents and dynamically constructed interpreter paths are outside complete coverage.

docs.title: Capy Hooks
docs.text:
Toolbox's session and Bash hooks stand in for capy's guidance and HTTP routing: session-start.sh injects .capy/AGENTS.md into the session context, and pretooluse-bash.sh denies curl, wget, and inline HTTP calls so the model routes them through capy's MCP tools.

Capy v0.17.1 and later ships its own Codex hooks. Running capy setup --platform codex in the project registers them in .codex/hooks.json next to toolbox's entries. They deliver availability-aware guidance and HTTP routing (advisory by default, evidence-based redirects, a silent-download exception) that toolbox's unconditional deny would otherwise override. Toolbox detects those entries per event — a registered command that invokes capy codex-launch — and steps aside:

  • session-start.sh replaces the .capy/AGENTS.md injection with a one-line note that capy's hooks own guidance and routing. Provider instructions and .claude/CLAUDE.*.md extras are still injected.
  • pretooluse-bash.sh skips the HTTP denials. The shared secrets, destructive-command and self-modification checks always run first. Ordinary reads of build output, .git/ and .env.example are allowed.

The check runs on every session start and every shell call, so there is no flag to flip and nothing to roll back. Remove capy's entries from hooks.json and the legacy behavior returns on the next session.

Remove capy's entries, don't disable them

Codex trusts hooks individually through /hooks, and capy's setup never changes trust. A capy entry that is present but disabled still makes toolbox step aside, so the project ends up with no capy guidance and no HTTP routing at all. To switch capy's Codex hooks off, delete its entries from .codex/hooks.json. After running setup, review and trust the new entries in /hooks; registration alone does not execute them.

docs.title: Template sync and capy's entries
docs.text:
Template sync does not own capy's registration. The template ships no [mcp_servers] table in config.toml and only toolbox's own entries in hooks.json; on every sync the downstream copies of both files are merged rather than replaced:

  • config.toml: toolbox substitutes model and approval_policy from the manifest, then keeps every mcp_servers.* entry the project has that the template does not ship. A server the template does ship wins by name. Existing explicit server tables whose values are unchanged are preserved byte-for-byte, including comments, ordering, quoting, nested tables, and whitespace. Only changed or repaired registrations are rendered as new explicit root-level tables, which capy setup can update.
  • hooks.json: toolbox owns every entry whose command runs a script under .codex/scripts/, and those come from the template verbatim, so a toolbox entry that changed or was removed upstream does not linger. Every other entry the project has (capy's capy codex-launch hooks, hand-added hooks) is appended after toolbox's entries for its event.
  • .codex/capy-owner: a built-in sync exclusion, never reported as deleted or removed. Capy refuses to regenerate a lost marker, so keep it committed alongside hooks.json and config.toml as capy's setup instructs.

The merge is stateless and derived from the project's files on every run. If either downstream file fails to parse, sync warns and falls back to the template copy for that file, which drops capy's entries; rerun capy setup --platform codex after fixing the file.

Older syncs could append an inline mcp_servers = { ... } assignment after [tui], making it part of the TUI settings instead of a root-level registration. Sync now recovers those misplaced servers into root-level tables. If capy setup has already added a valid root-level entry, that whole entry takes precedence over the misplaced copy. Applying sync removes the stray TUI assignment; no manual cleanup is needed.

Sync does not run capy setup. Preserving existing table text avoids formatting churn when alternating setup and sync. Table extraction uses Python 3's standard library; yq validates the extracted registrations and the complete merged MCP map before the candidate file is accepted.

docs.title: Shared guard support for capy execution
docs.text:
The shared permission-guard engine recognizes capy_execute, capy_execute_file, and capy_batch_execute under any MCP server name. It checks shell code like Bash, other-language code with its literal-path/write-call scans, and each batch command independently. An execute-file input receives the secrets Read check before its processing code is inspected.

Capy execution defaults to the project root. A supplied cwd is absolute or project-relative; it does not change the project identity or the anchor for capy_execute_file.path. The file input always remains project-root-relative. Path parameters are literal, without shell-variable or tilde expansion.

The template registers pretooluse-mcp.sh for these three tools, under any MCP server name. Capy's own registered hooks remain independent; a denial from either blocks the call.

docs.title: Permission Guard
docs.text:
For an existing installation, follow the permission-guard upgrade checklist: sync the project, review/trust new or changed hooks, then restart. The Codex plugin alone does not deliver this guard runtime.

All three adapters export the repository root before delegating to the generated engine. Relative Bash and patch paths resolve against the hook payload's cwd, while project policy remains anchored at the repository root. The guard inspects patch add, update, delete and move headers, including both sides of a move; it does not interpret patch contents as commands. Deleting a file is filesystem-destructive, with the engine's temporary-directory exemption and user category setting applied after secrets and self-modification checks.

Denials return JSON plus a reason on stderr and exit 2. Adapter errors and missing interpreters also block. Session startup renders a protected-files advisory from the synced declaration, falling back to a static secret-files warning if it is unavailable. See the guard rules and configuration for project additions and user exceptions. Maintainers regenerate the copied engine with make generate-guard; consumers receive it through template sync. Never edit .codex/scripts/guard/ directly.

The adapter contract targets Codex 0.164.0. The official hooks reference documents Edit|Write aliases, tool_input.command, and exit-2 denial with stderr. Hook coverage is a guardrail; specialized paths can bypass it. A live 0.164.0 probe on 2026-10-26 verified project-file registration from a repository subdirectory: SessionStart ran, the patch hook allowed a benign relative path, and the guard denied a synthetic .env addition. No inline hook registration was used.

After template setup, trust the project, then inspect and trust the hook definitions in /hooks. These are separate checks: a trusted project makes its .codex/ layer eligible for loading; hook trust permits the discovered handlers to run. Restart after trusting startup hooks. For diagnostics, the app-server's config/read and hooks/list methods expose config layers, hook source paths, enabled state, trust status and loading errors. Check invocation evidence as well as registration. The live probe used the one-invocation --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust flag for vetted scratch hooks; it did not verify the interactive trust workflow or change persisted trust.

Avoid codex exec --ignore-user-config when validating this integration on 0.164.0. In the tested scratch setup, that launch produced no project startup or patch-hook records, even with explicit project trust and -c 'features.hooks=true'; normal config loading invoked both hooks. This is an observed limitation of that invocation, not a claim that the flag universally disables project config. Isolate unrelated MCP servers or plugins with targeted overrides instead, retaining normal config loading.

Parity gap Reason Mitigation Native read_file secrets protection remains advisory This integration does not register or map native read payloads; earlier Codex versions did not intercept them (ADR 0005) Current secrets list in session context; optional sandbox permission profile remains pending Literal rm has no temporary-directory exemption; rm, shred, sudo, su, doas are not loosenable on Codex through guard user config Generated native forbids take precedence over user allow rules Run the operation yourself; repositories needing different native rules can exclude .codex/rules/default.rules from template sync and edit it Specialized/function-style apply_patch paths may bypass hooks Tool hooks are not a complete enforcement boundary Treat patch enforcement as limited to intercepted calls

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
Current limitations

  • Plugin-only installs provide skills and profile content only — hooks, sub-agents, rules, and project config require template setup or adopting into an existing repo.
  • Toolbox PreToolUse hooks cover Bash, intercepted apply_patch and capy's three execution tools. Native reads, specialized hook-bypassing paths and other execution tools are outside this integration's enforcement; see the parity table above.
  • MCP servers (Context7, Pal) must be configured at the user level — they are not packaged in the plugin. See Codex MCP Setup.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: claude-toolbox provides opinionated defaults for permissions, statusline, hooks, and project settings.

docs.title: How Configuration Works
docs.text:
Note

Claude Code settings are split between two project-scoped files:

  • .claude/settings.json — upstream-managed defaults, synced from this template (permissions baseline, env vars, model, plugins, statusline)
  • .claude/settings.local.json — your per-repo overrides, never synced (hooks, MCP server enables, additional permissions, personal preferences)

Use settings.local.json for personal settings. Template sync merges most settings, but replaces permissions.deny with the upstream secrets baseline and reports removed entries; permissions.allow remains union-merged. The guard protects both settings files from agent edits. A person can edit them directly, or enable the scoped disable_selfmod exception described below.

docs.title: Permission Baselines
docs.text:
The permission guard separates secrets, destructive operations and changes to its own configuration. Its baseline allows ordinary logs, dependencies, build output and .env.example; projects can add their own restrictions. A settings allow entry cannot override a secrets deny.

The tables below are generated from klaude-plugin/scripts/guard/guard-rules.json with make generate-guard. Template sync replaces permissions.deny with the secrets projection; project additions belong in .claude/kk-guard.json. See template sync for dropped-entry reports and the sync_exclusions opt-out. Per-repo MCP tool permissions go in settings.local.json.

Self-modification protection also blocks an agent from adding an allow entry to .claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.local.json. The disable_selfmod example below lets the user authorize those edits for a chosen project; it does not loosen secrets.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
These globs generate the Claude settings deny list and apply in the guard. Add project globs in .claude/kk-guard.json under secrets; user exceptions never loosen secrets.

Scope Glob Project ./**/*.pem Project ./**/*.tfstate Project ./**/*.tfstate.backup Project ./**/.env Project ./**/.env.*.local Project ./**/.env.local Project ./**/.terraform/** Project ./**/id_ecdsa Project ./**/id_ed25519 Project ./**/id_rsa Project ./**/service-account*.json Home ~/.aws/** Home ~/.claude/.credentials.json Home ~/.config/gcloud/** Home ~/.docker/config.json Home ~/.gnupg/** Home ~/.kube/** Home ~/.netrc Home ~/.pypirc Home ~/.ssh/**

docs.title: Protected configuration
docs.text:
The guard blocks mutations of these paths, including moving their parent directories:

  • .claude/settings.json
  • .claude/settings.local.json
  • .claude/kk-guard.json
  • ~/.claude/settings.json
  • ~/.claude/settings.local.json
  • ~/.claude/kk-guard.json
  • .codex/hooks.json
  • .codex/rules/**
  • .codex/scripts/**
  • ~/.claude/plugins/**

Project config may add paths under selfmod. To let an agent edit settings or guard files for one checkout, the user can add this entry to ~/.claude/kk-guard.json (substitute the absolute project path):

{"version":1,"projects":{"/absolute/path/to/repo":{"disable_selfmod":true}}}

This exception does not allow reading or writing secrets.

docs.title: Guard Configuration
docs.text:
The baseline ships inside the Claude plugin and runs even when neither configuration file exists. The Codex template carries the same engine and declaration. These files are independent of provider permission settings:

File Owner and purpose <project>/.claude/kk-guard.json Committed project restrictions; adds secrets globs, destructive rules or protected paths ~/.claude/kk-guard.json Machine owner's exceptions; loosens destructive categories or self-modification protection for selected projects

docs.title: Project restrictions
docs.text:
Project configuration only adds protection. For example:

{
  "version": 1,
  "secrets": ["./**/local-secrets.json"],
  "selfmod": [".project-policy.json"],
  "destructive": {
    "deployment": [
      {"program": "deploy", "subcommand": "prod", "reason": "deploy prod changes production"}
    ]
  }
}

Secrets globs use ./**/ for project paths, ~/ for home paths, or // for absolute paths. They match requested and resolved paths. Project-relative policy stays anchored to the project root even when a shell runs in a subdirectory. Destructive rules use program, optional ordered subcommand, argument regex lists flags_any/flags_all/flags_none, and a reason; use the shipped declaration as the complete rule reference. The only supported named exemption is targets_under_tmp. Project config cannot disable categories or remove baseline rules. Template sync leaves this project-owned file alone.

docs.title: User exceptions
docs.text:
The user edits this file directly; the guard protects it from agent writes. Merge entries into an existing projects object rather than replacing other project entries. For example:

{
  "version": 1,
  "projects": {
    "*": {"allow_patterns": ["^git clean -n"]},
    "/absolute/path/to/ops": {"disable_categories": ["infra"]},
    "/absolute/path/to/claude-toolbox": {"disable_selfmod": true}
  }
}

Use physical absolute project paths (pwd -P). The engine combines * with the single longest matching directory prefix; shorter matching prefixes contribute nothing. Lists are combined, and disable_selfmod is enabled if either selected entry enables it. A parent path covers nested repositories and worktrees.

allow_patterns applies separately to each normalized simple command, including extracted shell bodies. Thus ^git clean -n can exempt git clean -nd, but not the rm in git clean -nd; rm -rf ./work. These patterns never exempt secrets or protected configuration. disable_selfmod permits settings/guard edits only; it also leaves secrets protected. On Codex, native forbids for rm, shred, sudo, su and doas still win over guard exceptions.

Missing config files leave the baseline active. Invalid JSON or invalid supported values produce a visible systemMessage and skip that file's changes; the other valid layer still applies. Unknown keys are reported and ignored. Secrets are never loosened by user configuration.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
The Claude plugin ships two hooks. It needs Bash, jq, Python 3.8+ and Claude Code 2.1.295+ for the declared onFailure: "block" behavior.

Hook Trigger Description Plugin root export SessionStart Exports TOOLBOX_PLUGIN_ROOT into the session environment so every Bash call has a reliable path to the plugin installation directory Permission guard PreToolUse on Bash, Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit, and capy execution tools Enforces secrets, destructive-command rules, and protected configuration paths; denies on guard failures

Ordinary allowed calls produce no output and exit 0; invalid-config warnings may emit systemMessage. Denials emit JSON, a reason on stderr, and exit 2. Missing/broken interpreters, a corrupt declaration, crashes and malformed engine output deny the call. Claude also blocks hook failures/timeouts through onFailure: "block". A machine without a working Python interpreter blocks every matched tool, including reads, until repaired.

Codex adapters preserve the guard's denial reason and exit status. A normal policy denial does not mean the hook needs repair; the separate "adapter could not run" diagnostic indicates an adapter failure, such as a missing guard wrapper or unreadable hook input.

The wrapper runs the standard-library-only engine with -I -S, isolating Python environment/user-site settings and skipping unused site startup. On macOS it prefers Python at the standard Homebrew locations, then system Python; elsewhere it checks system Python first. PATH lookup remains the final fallback. Homebrew is not required.

Destructive operations are denied in every permission mode, including bypass mode. The reason names the matched category and the way through: the user runs the operation directly or configures an applicable exception. Disabling Claude hooks removes destructive and self-modification protection. Template users retain the native secrets settings baseline; plugin-only users have no such fallback.

The guard checks capy_execute, capy_execute_file, and capy_batch_execute even when capy is registered under a different MCP server name. Shell code uses the same checks as Bash; other languages use the existing literal-path and write-call scans. Every batch command is checked independently, and one denied command blocks the entire batch before execution.

For capy code, omitted cwd means the project root. Relative cwd overrides resolve from that root; absolute overrides select that directory. Each batch command starts in the selected directory. The capy_execute_file.path input stays project-root-relative regardless of where its processing code runs. These path parameters are literal paths, without shell-variable or tilde expansion.

Inspection is static: the guard does not execute submitted code or read the contents of an execute-file input. Paths assembled dynamically are outside its detection coverage, and non-shell mutation checks cover recognized literal write-call forms. Grep/Glob checks cover the search root, not every result's contents. Other execution tools need their own payload mapping. The Codex template supplies Bash, patch and capy adapters; see Codex limitations.

For shell paths, the guard retains possible directories after literal relative changes and checks existing matches of unquoted filename wildcards. Quoted or escaped wildcard characters remain literal. Interpreter checks decode common character escapes in literal paths while preserving raw strings. These checks inspect filenames and submitted text, without executing code or reading matched file contents.

• CLAUDE.md — project-specific instructions for Claude Code (checked into the repo)
  • .claude/CLAUDE.extra.md — behavioral instructions (independent thinking, fail-loud, assumptions)
